mcqs.q: Phase I therapy occupies which position in the sequence of periodontal treatment?
opts: The first in the chronologic sequence of procedures
The second, after the emergency phase has been completed
The last, after all surgical procedures are finished
It runs in parallel with the surgical phase throughout
mcqs.explain: It is the first in the chronologic sequence that constitutes periodontal treatment.

mcqs.q: The objective of phase I therapy is to alter or eliminate the microbial etiology and contributing factors, thereby:
opts: Halting the progression of disease and returning the dentition to health and comfort
Regenerating the lost periodontal ligament and alveolar bone
Preparing the pockets for immediate surgical elimination
Eradicating all bacteria from the subgingival environment
mcqs.explain: Halting progression and returning the dentition to a state of health and comfort is the stated objective.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT another name for phase I therapy?
opts: Maintenance therapy
Initial therapy
Nonsurgical periodontal therapy
Cause-related therapy
mcqs.explain: Initial, nonsurgical and cause-related therapy are the alternative names given.

mcqs.q: The AAP evidence-based definition of phase I therapy includes all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Surgical elimination of all pockets deeper than 5 mm
Initiation of a comprehensive daily plaque or biofilm control regimen
Management of periodontal-systemic interrelationships as needed
Thorough removal of supragingival and subgingival plaque and calculus
mcqs.explain: Pocket surgery belongs to the surgical phase, not to phase I.

mcqs.q: Besides biofilm control and debridement, which other problems must be managed in phase I therapy?
opts: Chemotherapeutic agents as necessary, and local factors such as defective restorations and caries
Occlusal rehabilitation and implant placement
Orthognathic correction of the skeletal relationship
Endodontic retreatment of all restored teeth
mcqs.explain: Chemotherapeutic agents, defective restorations and carious lesions are the additional problems listed.

mcqs.q: The approach of phase I therapy is aimed at removal of pathogenic biofilms, toxins and calculus, and:
opts: Re-establishment of a biologically acceptable root surface
Complete sterilisation of the periodontal pocket
Surgical recontouring of the alveolar crest
Elimination of the junctional epithelium
mcqs.explain: A biologically acceptable root surface is the goal of root instrumentation.

mcqs.q: Long-term success of periodontal SURGICAL treatment depends on:
opts: Maintaining the plaque control results achieved with phase I therapy
The flap design chosen at the time of surgery
The suture material used to close the flap
The depth of the pockets recorded before phase I therapy
mcqs.explain: Surgical results are only as durable as the biofilm control that follows.

mcqs.q: A patient who does not achieve adequate plaque control will:
opts: Continue to lose attachment regardless of the surgical procedures performed
Lose attachment only if the surgery was incorrectly performed
Maintain attachment provided the surgery eliminated the pockets
Lose attachment only at sites that were never surgically treated
mcqs.explain: Inadequate biofilm control defeats any surgical procedure.

mcqs.q: Apart from its therapeutic effect, phase I therapy also gives the dentist the opportunity to:
opts: Evaluate tissue response and reinforce home care
Establish the definitive occlusal scheme
Measure bone levels without radiographs
Determine the patient's microbial profile
mcqs.explain: Both tissue-response evaluation and home-care reinforcement are crucial to overall success.

mcqs.q: Because microbial biofilm is the major etiologic agent in gingival inflammation, the specific aim of phase I therapy for EVERY patient is:
opts: Effective daily plaque or biofilm removal at home
Quarterly professional scaling in the clinic
Long-term systemic antibiotic coverage
Daily rinsing with a chemotherapeutic agent
mcqs.explain: Daily home biofilm removal is the aim for every patient, whatever else is planned.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is one of the nine elements of phase I therapy?
opts: Extraction of hopeless teeth
Placement of a free gingival graft
Guided tissue regeneration of vertical defects
Apically positioned flap surgery
mcqs.explain: Extraction of hopeless teeth is element 8; the others are surgical procedures.

mcqs.q: Orthodontic tooth movement and treatment of food impaction areas are:
opts: Both elements of phase I therapy
Both part of the surgical phase
Both deferred to the maintenance phase
Both excluded from periodontal treatment planning
mcqs.explain: They are elements 5 and 6 of the nine listed.

mcqs.q: Which patient-related factor must be considered when determining the phase I treatment plan?
opts: General health and tolerance of treatment
The brand of toothpaste the patient uses
The patient's previous orthodontic history only
The number of radiographs previously taken
mcqs.explain: General health, tolerance of treatment and patient cooperation head the list.

mcqs.q: A limited mouth opening or a tendency to gag is classified among the phase I planning considerations as:
opts: A physical barrier to access the dentition
A contraindication to any periodontal therapy
A developmental anomaly
An indication for immediate specialist referral
mcqs.explain: Physical barriers to access are explicitly listed among the conditions to consider.

mcqs.q: Plaque control instruction should begin:
opts: At the first treatment appointment
At the reevaluation appointment four weeks later
After all calculus has been removed
Only once the gingival inflammation has resolved
mcqs.explain: Instruction starts at the very first treatment appointment.

mcqs.q: Before oral hygiene instruction is given, the patient must first:
opts: Understand the reason he or she must actively participate in therapy
Demonstrate an acceptable brushing technique
Have all calculus professionally removed
Agree in writing to a surgical treatment plan
mcqs.explain: Explaining the aetiology makes teaching the technique easier and more durable.

mcqs.q: The term used for instructing a patient in the correct technique to remove plaque from his or her own problem areas is:
opts: Targeted oral hygiene
Supervised debridement
Full-mouth disinfection
Chemotherapeutic control
mcqs.explain: Targeted oral hygiene is the term used for this individualised instruction.

mcqs.q: Interdental cleaning instruction in phase I therapy covers:
opts: Dental floss and interdental brushes
Oral irrigation devices only
Wooden sticks and rubber tips only
Chlorhexidine rinsing in place of mechanical cleaning
mcqs.explain: Floss and interdental brushes are the methods named.

mcqs.q: Oral hygiene skills are best developed through:
opts: Numerous appointments to evaluate, reinforce and improve them
A single thorough demonstration at the first visit
Written instructions handed to the patient to read at home
Deferring instruction until after reevaluation
mcqs.explain: Repeated appointments allow evaluation, reinforcement and improvement.

mcqs.q: Removal of calculus and root planing is accomplished using:
opts: Scalers, curettes, ultrasonic instrumentation, or combinations of these
Curettes alone, since powered devices damage cementum
Ultrasonic instrumentation alone, since hand instruments are obsolete
Rotary burs in a high-speed handpiece
mcqs.explain: Any of these, singly or combined, over one or more appointments.

mcqs.q: Photodynamic therapy as an adjunct to scaling and root planing uses lasers at specific wavelengths to:
opts: Target microorganisms treated with a photosensitizer
Vaporise the calculus deposits on the root surface
Coagulate the inflamed pocket epithelium
Stimulate osteoblasts in the alveolar crest
mcqs.explain: The photosensitizer is what makes the microorganisms susceptible to the light.

mcqs.q: In the full-mouth disinfection technique, treatment is performed:
opts: During one session, or multiple sessions within a few days
Quadrant by quadrant at weekly intervals
Over six months in a staged protocol
Only after the reevaluation appointment
mcqs.explain: Compressing the treatment into a short window is the essence of the technique.

mcqs.q: Disinfectants are used after full-mouth disinfection with the intention of:
opts: Preventing reinfection of treated sites from untreated sites
Dissolving residual subgingival calculus
Reducing post-operative root sensitivity
Accelerating connective tissue reattachment
mcqs.explain: Cross-contamination from untreated to treated sites is what the protocol is designed to prevent.

mcqs.q: Defective restorations are a problem in periodontal therapy because they are:
opts: Plaque or biofilm retentive areas
A direct source of bacterial toxins
A cause of occlusal trauma in every case
An absolute contraindication to scaling
mcqs.explain: Their roughness and overhangs retain biofilm, which is why they are corrected in phase I.

mcqs.q: Overhangs on faulty restorations are corrected by:
opts: Smoothing with burs or hand instruments, or complete replacement if needed
Surgical crown lengthening in every case
Chemical dissolution with an acidic conditioner
Leaving them until after the surgical phase
mcqs.explain: Smoothing and overhang removal, or replacing the failing restoration, are the options.

mcqs.q: Carious lesions are managed within phase I therapy because of:
opts: The infectious nature of the carious process
The risk of pulpal exposure during scaling
The need to restore occlusal vertical dimension first
Insurance requirements for staged treatment
mcqs.explain: Caries is an infection, and the lesion is a bacterial reservoir.

mcqs.q: Removing carious lesions maximises periodontal healing by:
opts: Removing a reservoir of bacteria that could repopulate the plaque
Reducing the occlusal load on the affected teeth
Allowing deeper penetration of the periodontal probe
Permitting the use of ultrasonic instrumentation
mcqs.explain: Without the reservoir, the treated sites cannot be re-seeded from the lesion.

mcqs.q: After scaling, root planing and other phase I procedures, how long do the periodontal tissues need to heal before reevaluation?
opts: Approximately 4 weeks
Approximately 1 week
Approximately 2 weeks
Approximately 12 weeks
mcqs.explain: Four weeks allows connective tissue healing so that accurate probing depths can be measured.

mcqs.q: The reason reevaluation is delayed rather than performed immediately is that the waiting period:
opts: Allows the connective tissues to heal so accurate probe depths can be measured
Permits the patient to recover from the anaesthesia
Gives time for radiographic bone fill to appear
Allows the microbial flora to be resampled
mcqs.explain: Probing an unhealed site gives a falsely deep reading.

mcqs.q: Additional improvement from periodontal surgery can be expected ONLY IF phase I therapy has produced:
opts: Gingival tissues free of overt inflammation and effective daily plaque control by the patient
Probing depths of 3 mm or less at every site
Complete radiographic resolution of the bone defects
A full-mouth bleeding score of zero
mcqs.explain: Both conditions — resolved inflammation and patient-performed control — must be met.

mcqs.q: Scaling and root planing produces mean probing depth reductions of:
opts: 2 to 3 mm
1 mm or less
4 to 5 mm
More than 5 mm
mcqs.explain: Reduced bleeding on probing and 2–3 mm mean depth reduction are the reported results.

mcqs.q: Caries control and correction of poorly fitting restorations help the healing gained by debridement mainly by:
opts: Making tooth surfaces accessible to hygiene procedures
Reducing the virulence of the subgingival microbiota
Increasing the patient's salivary buffering capacity
Stimulating regeneration of the periodontal ligament
mcqs.explain: Accessibility to home-care procedures is what these corrections deliver.

mcqs.q: Maximal healing from phase I treatment is NOT possible when:
opts: Local conditions retain biofilm and provide reservoirs for repopulation of pathogens
The patient is older than sixty years
The probing depths exceed 4 mm at any site
The treatment is completed in more than one appointment
mcqs.explain: Retentive local conditions keep re-seeding the treated sites.

mcqs.q: Healing after phase I therapy is characterised by the formation of:
opts: A long junctional epithelium rather than new connective tissue attachment
A new connective tissue attachment to the instrumented root
New cementum with inserting Sharpey's fibres
A fibrous scar that obliterates the sulcus
mcqs.explain: Nonsurgical therapy heals by a long junctional epithelium, not true reattachment.

mcqs.q: The long junctional epithelium forms approximately:
opts: 1 week after therapy
1 day after therapy
4 weeks after therapy
3 months after therapy
mcqs.explain: Epithelial healing is fast — about one week; connective tissue takes four weeks or more.

mcqs.q: How much recession is often apparent after phase I therapy as a result of tissue shrinkage?
opts: 1 to 2 mm
Less than 0.5 mm
3 to 4 mm
More than 5 mm
mcqs.explain: One to two millimetres of recession is an expected consequence, not a complication.

mcqs.q: Connective tissue fibres require how long to reorganise and heal after phase I therapy?
opts: Four or more weeks
One week
Two weeks
Twenty-four hours
mcqs.explain: Many cases require several weeks beyond this for complete healing.

mcqs.q: Which symptom frequently accompanies the healing process after phase I therapy?
opts: Transient root sensitivity
Persistent spontaneous pain
Progressive tooth mobility
Altered taste sensation
mcqs.explain: Root sensitivity after instrumentation is common and transient.

mcqs.q: Many periodontally involved cases:
opts: Do not require any therapy beyond phase I and can be maintained by a general dentist
Require surgical intervention regardless of the response to phase I
Must be referred to a specialist before phase I is begun
Cannot be assessed until surgical access has been obtained
mcqs.explain: Routine maintenance by the general dentist suffices for many patients.

mcqs.q: The critical probing depth that has been advanced to assist the decision to proceed to surgery is:
opts: 5.4 mm
3.0 mm
4.5 mm
6.5 mm
mcqs.explain: Above it, therapy results in attachment gain; below it, attachment loss.

mcqs.q: Above the critical probing depth, periodontal therapy will result in:
opts: Clinical attachment gain
Clinical attachment loss
No measurable change in attachment
Progressive gingival recession only
mcqs.explain: Below the critical depth, instrumentation costs more attachment than it gains.

mcqs.q: The practical 5-mm standard for surgical referral assumes a typical root length of:
opts: About 13 mm
About 10 mm
About 16 mm
About 20 mm
mcqs.explain: A 13 mm root, with the bone crest about 2 mm apical to the pocket base, underlies the standard.

mcqs.q: In the 5-mm standard, the crest of the alveolar bone is assumed to lie:
opts: Approximately 2 mm apical to the bottom of the pocket
Level with the bottom of the pocket
Approximately 5 mm apical to the bottom of the pocket
Approximately 2 mm coronal to the bottom of the pocket
mcqs.explain: This 2 mm offset is why a 5 mm pocket implies a crest 7 mm from the CEJ.

mcqs.q: When there is 5 mm of clinical attachment loss, the bone crest is about 7 mm from the CEJ, which means that:
opts: Only about half of the bony support for the tooth remains
About a quarter of the bony support has been lost
The tooth has lost all of its bony support
The bony support is unaffected at this stage
mcqs.explain: Seven of the thirteen millimetres is gone, leaving roughly half the support.

mcqs.q: In such cases, periodontal surgery can improve support through:
opts: Pocket reduction, bone augmentation and regeneration procedures
Occlusal adjustment and splinting alone
Systemic antibiotic therapy alone
Extraction and immediate implant placement
mcqs.explain: These three surgical avenues are the ones named.

mcqs.q: Short-rooted teeth are relevant to the referral decision because they:
opts: Are jeopardized to a greater extent by the 5-mm attachment loss criterion
Are easier to instrument so rarely need referral
Have a better response to regeneration procedures
Are never candidates for surgical therapy
mcqs.explain: The same 5 mm of loss removes a larger proportion of a short root's support.

mcqs.q: Excessive tooth mobility in the referral decision suggests that:
opts: Contributing factors may be responsible, and the prognosis may be guarded to poor
The tooth should be extracted without further assessment
Scaling and root planing is contraindicated
The disease must be grade A
mcqs.explain: Hypermobility points to contributing factors and a guarded-to-poor prognosis.

mcqs.q: Deep pockets and furcations make instrumentation difficult, but the results can often be improved with:
opts: Surgical access
A longer course of systemic antibiotics
More frequent prophylaxis appointments
A change of toothbrush design
mcqs.explain: Surgical access is what overcomes the instrumentation difficulty.

mcqs.q: Younger patients with extensive attachment loss are more likely to:
opts: Have aggressive forms of disease requiring advanced therapy
Respond completely to phase I therapy alone
Have a grade A rate of progression
Require only maintenance therapy
mcqs.explain: Extensive loss at a young age signals a rapid rate of progression.

mcqs.q: If inflammation and progressive pocket deepening continue despite thorough plaque removal and excellent scaling and root planing, then:
opts: Further therapy is necessary and the etiology must be understood
The plaque control must simply be repeated unchanged
The case should be placed on routine maintenance
The findings can be attributed to probing error
mcqs.explain: Lack of resolution after correct therapy is factor 7 in the referral decision.

mcqs.q: Rapid progression of disease corresponds to which grade, and requires what action?
opts: Grade C — timely referral to a periodontist
Grade A — continued maintenance by the general dentist
Grade B — a repeat course of scaling and root planing
Grade C — immediate extraction of the affected teeth
mcqs.explain: Grade C periodontitis needs proper referral in a timely fashion for effective management.

mcqs.q: Which defects have a better prognosis with regeneration approaches when treated early?
opts: Vertical defects with multiple walls and early furcation defects in molars
Horizontal bone loss of the coronal third
Class III through-and-through furcations
Generalized one-wall craters
mcqs.explain: Multiple-walled vertical defects and early furcation defects are the regenerable ones named.

mcqs.q: For patients who do require surgical intervention, phase I therapy is advantageous because it:
opts: Permits tissue healing, improving surgical management and the healing response
Eliminates the need for local anaesthesia at surgery
Removes the need for post-surgical maintenance
Reduces the number of teeth requiring surgical access
mcqs.explain: Healed, non-inflamed tissue handles better and heals better after surgery.

saqs.q: Define phase I periodontal therapy, state its objective, and give its alternative names.
saqs.a: Phase I therapy, or cause-related therapy, is the first in the chronologic sequence of procedures that constitute periodontal treatment. Its objective is to alter or eliminate the microbial etiology and the factors that contribute to gingival and periodontal diseases to the greatest extent possible, thereby halting the progression of disease and returning the dentition to a state of health and comfort. It is also called initial therapy, nonsurgical periodontal therapy and cause-related therapy.

list: The first in the chronologic sequence of procedures that constitute periodontal treatment.
To alter or eliminate the microbial etiology and the contributing factors to the greatest extent possible.
Thereby halting the progression of disease and returning the dentition to a state of health and comfort.
Initial therapy
Nonsurgical periodontal therapy
Cause-related therapy

saqs.q: Give the AAP evidence-based definition of phase I therapy and the other problems it must manage.
saqs.a: It is the initiation of a comprehensive daily plaque or biofilm control regimen, management of periodontal-systemic interrelationships as needed, and thorough removal of supragingival and subgingival bacterial plaque or biofilm and calculus. Other problems to manage are the use of chemotherapeutic agents as necessary and local factors such as elimination of defective restorations and treatment of carious lesions. The approach aims at removal of pathogenic biofilms, toxins and calculus and the re-establishment of a biologically acceptable root surface.

list: Initiation of a comprehensive daily plaque or biofilm control regimen.
Management of periodontal–systemic interrelationships as needed.
Thorough removal of supragingival and subgingival plaque or biofilm and calculus.
Use of chemotherapeutic agents as necessary.
Local factors — elimination of defective restorations, treatment of carious lesions.

ans.text: The approach is aimed at removal of pathogenic biofilms, toxins and calculus, and the re-establishment of a biologically acceptable root surface.

saqs.q: Why is phase I therapy the basis for periodontal surgery?
saqs.a: Long-term success of periodontal surgical treatment depends on maintaining the plaque control results achieved with phase I therapy. Patients without adequate plaque control will continue to lose attachment regardless of the surgical procedures performed. Phase I therapy also gives the dentist an opportunity to evaluate tissue response and reinforce home care, both crucial to the overall success of treatment.

list: Long-term success of surgery depends on maintaining the biofilm control achieved in phase I.
Patients without adequate control continue to lose attachment regardless of the surgery performed.
It gives an opportunity to evaluate tissue response and reinforce home care.

saqs.q: List the nine elements that make up phase I therapy.
saqs.a: Patient education and oral hygiene instruction; complete removal of calculus; correction or replacement of poorly fitting restorations and other prosthetic devices; restoration or temporization of carious lesions; orthodontic tooth movement; treatment of food impaction areas; treatment of occlusal trauma; extraction of hopeless teeth; and possible use of antimicrobial agents.

list: 1. Patient education and oral hygiene instruction
2. Complete removal of calculus
3. Correction or replacement of poorly fitting restorations and other prosthetic devices
4. Restoration or temporization of carious lesions
5. Orthodontic tooth movement
6. Treatment of food impaction areas
7. Treatment of occlusal trauma
8. Extraction of hopeless teeth
9. Possible use of antimicrobial agents

saqs.q: What conditions must be considered when determining the phase I treatment plan?
saqs.a: General health and tolerance of treatment; number of teeth present; amount of subgingival calculus; probing pocket depths; attachment loss; furcation involvement; alignment of teeth; margins of restorations; developmental anomalies; physical barriers to access the dentition such as limited opening or a tendency to gag; and patient cooperation and sensitivity to therapy requiring anaesthesia or analgesia.

head: Group
Factors
rows: general health and tolerance of treatment; cooperation and sensitivity to therapy (anaesthesia or analgesia)
amount of subgingival calculus; probing pocket depths; attachment loss; furcation involvement
physical barriers — limited opening, tendency to gag

saqs.q: List the five steps in the sequence of phase I procedures.
saqs.a: Step 1 plaque or biofilm control instruction; Step 2 removal of supragingival and subgingival plaque or biofilm and calculus; Step 3 recontouring defective restorations and crowns; Step 4 management of carious lesions; Step 5 tissue reevaluation.

steps: Step 2 — removal of supragingival and subgingival plaque or biofilm and calculus

saqs.q: Describe Step 1, plaque or biofilm control instruction.
saqs.a: Instruction begins at the first treatment appointment. The patient must first understand why he or she must actively participate, so the etiology of the disease is explained; once the nature and etiology are understood it is easier to teach the required hygiene. The patient is instructed in the correct technique to remove plaque — targeted oral hygiene — and in interdental cleaning with floss and interdental brushes. Numerous appointments are used to evaluate, reinforce and improve the patient's skills.

list: Instruction begins at the first treatment appointment.
The patient must first understand why he or she must actively participate — the etiology is explained first.
Instruct in the correct technique to remove plaque — targeted oral hygiene.
Initiate interdental cleaning with dental floss and interdental brushes.
Use numerous appointments to evaluate, reinforce and improve the skills.

saqs.q: Describe Step 2, including the adjunctive approaches mentioned.
saqs.a: Removal of calculus and root planing is accomplished using scalers, curettes, ultrasonic instrumentation or combinations of these, over one or more appointments. Laser treatment has been advocated. Photodynamic therapy is an adjunct using lasers at specific wavelengths to target microorganisms treated with a photosensitizer. Full-mouth disinfection delivers full-mouth treatment in one session or several within a few days, with disinfectants used afterwards to prevent reinfection of treated sites from untreated sites.

list: Scalers, curettes, ultrasonic instrumentation, or combinations — over one or more appointments.
Laser treatment has also been advocated.
Photodynamic therapy — lasers at specific wavelengths to target microorganisms treated with a photosensitizer.
Full-mouth disinfection — full-mouth treatment in one session or several within a few days, with disinfectants afterwards to prevent reinfection of treated sites from untreated sites.

saqs.q: Describe Steps 3 and 4 of phase I therapy.
saqs.a: Step 3 recontours defective restorations and crowns, which are plaque retentive areas: rough surfaces are smoothed and overhangs removed with burs or hand instruments, or the failing restoration is completely replaced. Step 4 manages carious lesions: they are removed and restored temporarily or permanently because of the infectious nature of the carious process, since removing the reservoir of bacteria prevents them repopulating the plaque and maximises periodontal healing.

ans.h: Step 3 — recontouring defective restorations and crowns
list: Restorative defects are plaque or biofilm retentive areas.
Smooth rough surfaces and remove overhangs with burs or hand instruments, or completely replace the failing restoration.
Remove the lesions and place temporary or permanent restorations, because of the infectious nature of caries.
Healing is maximised by removing the reservoir of bacteria so they cannot repopulate the plaque.

saqs.a: The periodontal tissues need approximately four weeks to heal, which allows the connective tissues to heal so that accurate probe depths can be measured. At the reevaluation appointment the tissues are probed and all related anatomic conditions evaluated to decide whether further treatment, including periodontal surgery, is indicated. Additional improvement from surgery can be expected only if phase I therapy has produced gingival tissues free of overt inflammation and the patient has adopted effective daily plaque control.

list: The tissues require approximately 4 weeks to heal — allowing connective tissue healing and accurate probe depths.
At reevaluation the tissues are probed and all related anatomic conditions evaluated, to decide whether further treatment including surgery is indicated.

ans.text: Additional improvement from surgery can be expected ONLY IF phase I produced gingival tissues free of overt inflammation AND the patient has adopted effective daily plaque control.

saqs.q: State the results of phase I therapy.
saqs.a: Scaling and root planing is both effective and reliable, giving a reduction in bleeding on probing and mean probing depth reductions of 2 to 3 mm. Additional individual treatments such as caries control and correction of poorly fitting restorations help the healing gained by good plaque control and debridement by making tooth surfaces accessible to hygiene procedures. Maximal healing is not possible when local conditions retain biofilm and provide reservoirs for repopulation of periodontal pathogens.

list: Scaling and root planing is effective and reliable.
Reduction in bleeding on probing, and mean probing depth reductions of 2 to 3 mm.
Caries control and correction of restorations help by making tooth surfaces accessible to hygiene procedures.
Maximal healing is not possible when local conditions retain biofilm and provide reservoirs for repopulation.

saqs.q: Describe the healing that follows phase I therapy, with its timings.
saqs.a: Healing is by formation of a long junctional epithelium rather than new connective tissue attachment to the root, occurring about one week after therapy. Gradual reductions in inflammatory cell population and crevicular fluid flow, with repair of connective tissue, decrease the clinical signs of inflammation. One to two millimetres of recession is often apparent from tissue shrinkage. Connective tissue fibres require four or more weeks to reorganise and heal, and many cases need several weeks for complete healing. Transient root sensitivity frequently accompanies healing.

head: Event
Timing / amount
rows: Formation of a long junctional epithelium (not new connective tissue attachment)
Reduced inflammatory cells, crevicular fluid flow, connective tissue repair → less redness and swelling
Connective tissue fibres reorganise and heal

saqs.q: Explain the concept of the critical probing depth and the 5-mm standard for referral.
saqs.a: The critical probing depth of 5.4 mm is the measurement above which therapy will result in clinical attachment gain and below which it will result in clinical attachment loss. A similar 5-mm standard is used as a guideline for identifying candidates for surgical referral, based on a typical root length of about 13 mm and a bone crest about 2 mm apical to the bottom of the pocket. With 5 mm of clinical attachment loss the crest is about 7 mm apical to the CEJ, so only about half of the bony support remains; surgery can then improve support through pocket reduction, bone augmentation and regeneration.

list: Above it, therapy results in clinical attachment gain.
Below it, therapy results in clinical attachment loss.
Typical root length is about 13 mm; the bone crest lies about 2 mm apical to the bottom of the pocket.
With 5 mm of attachment loss the crest is about 7 mm from the CEJ — only about half the bony support remains.
Surgery can then improve support through pocket reduction, bone augmentation and regeneration.

saqs.q: List the nine factors, other than the 5-mm probing depth, that influence the decision to refer to a periodontal specialist.
saqs.a: Extent of the disease and generalized or localized involvement; root length; hypermobility; difficulty of scaling and root planing; restorability and importance of particular teeth for reconstruction; age of the patient; lack of resolution of inflammation after thorough plaque removal and excellent scaling and root planing; rapid progression of disease; and defects that can be regenerated.

head: Factor
Why it matters
rows: the amount of bone loss, even if localized, suggests the need for specialized surgical techniques
short-rooted teeth are jeopardized more by the 5-mm criterion
suggests contributing factors; prognosis may be guarded to poor
4. Difficulty of scaling and root planing
deep pockets and furcations — results improved with surgical access
long-term prognosis of each tooth matters before extensive restorative work
younger patients with extensive loss are more likely to have aggressive disease
continuing inflammation and progressive pocket deepening need further therapy
grade C periodontitis — timely referral to a periodontist
multi-walled vertical defects and early furcation defects do better with early regeneration

saqs.q: What are the concluding points about the role of phase I therapy in the overall treatment plan?
saqs.a: Every patient is unique and the decision process for each is complex and difficult. Many patients can attain periodontal disease control with phase I therapy alone and do not require further surgical intervention. For patients who do require surgery, phase I therapy is advantageous because it permits tissue healing, thus improving the surgical management and the healing response of the tissues.

list: Every patient is unique, and the decision process for each is complex and difficult.
Many patients attain disease control with phase I therapy alone, without further surgical intervention.
For those who do need surgery, phase I permits tissue healing, improving the surgical management and the healing response.
